title: Why Earth is nearly inertial
canonical_question: Why can Earth’s surface be treated as an approximately inertial frame despite its rotation?
summary: Earth rotates and orbits, so strictly its surface is a non-inertial frame.
Over large scales or long times the rotation shows up, for instance in the swing of a Foucault pendulum or the curving of winds.

reuse.rationale: Authored fixture node for the E05 registry.

sections.heading: Small accelerations
sections.body_md: Earth rotates and orbits, so strictly its surface is a non-inertial frame. But the accelerations these motions produce are tiny compared with everyday forces, so their effects usually go unnoticed. For most experiments the ground behaves as if inertial.

sections.heading: When the approximation breaks
sections.body_md: Over large scales or long times the rotation shows up, for instance in the swing of a Foucault pendulum or the curving of winds. There the small effects accumulate and the frame’s non-inertial nature becomes visible. Scale decides whether the approximation holds.

key_points: Earth is strictly non-inertial but nearly inertial.
Its accelerations are small day to day.
core.bridge_to_parent: It explains an approximation, not the definition test.

seeds: How do I decide if a frame is inertial at all?
